text: Westley Watende Omari Moore, born October 15, 1978, in Takoma Park, Maryland, is an American politician, businessman, author, and former U.S. Army officer who has served as the 63rd governor of Maryland since 2023. He is a member of the Democratic Party and became Maryland's first African-American governor and the third African-American person elected governor of any U.S. state in the 2022 election. Moore was raised primarily in New York after his father, William Westley Moore Jr., died of acute epiglottitis when he was three years old; his mother, Joy Thomas Moore, is the daughter of immigrants from Cuba and Jamaica and a news media professional. His maternal grandfather, James Thomas, was the first Black minister in the history of the Dutch Reformed Church, and his grandmother, Winell Thomas, a Cuban who moved to Jamaica before immigrating to the U.S., was a retired schoolteacher; her stepfather was Chinese. Moore attended Riverdale Country School and later Valley Forge Military Academy and College after his grades declined and he became involved in petty crime. He earned an associate degree from Valley Forge in 1998, completed the U.S. Army's early commissioning program, and was appointed a second lieutenant in the Army Reserve. He graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Johns Hopkins University in 2001 with a B.A. in international relations and economics, where he played wide receiver for the Blue Jays football team and served as chair of the Men of the NAACP branch. He interned for Baltimore Mayor Kurt Schmoke and at the U.S. Department of Homeland Security under Secretary Tom Ridge. As a Rhodes Scholar, he earned a master's degree in international relations from Wolfson College, Oxford in 2004, with a thesis titled "Rise and Ramifications of Radical Islam in the Western Hemisphere," and served in the 82nd Airborne Division, being deployed to Afghanistan from 2005 to 2006, attaining the rank of captain. He left the Army in 2014 and was named a White House Fellow to Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice in February 2006. He worked as an investment banker at Deutsche Bank and Citibank from 2007 to 2012. In 2010, he founded Omari Productions to create content for networks including OWN, PBS, HBO, and NBC. In May 2014, he produced the three-part PBS series "Coming Back with Wes Moore," which followed returning veterans. In 2014, he founded BridgeEdU, a company that provided services to support students in transitioning to college, with students paying $500 and varying fees; the company was acquired by Edquity in 2019, primarily for its client database, and had mixed results according to a Baltimore Banner interview. Moore was the commencement speaker at Utah Valley University's 2014 graduation. In September 2016, he produced the PBS documentary "All the Difference," following two young African-American men from Chicago through college, and launched the talk show "Future City" on WYPR. From June 2017 to May 2021, he served as CEO of the Robin Hood Foundation, a charitable organization that alleviates poverty in New York City through funding schools, food pantries, shelters, and a disaster relief fund; during his tenure, the organization raised over $650 million, including $230 million in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Prior to becoming governor, he was on the boards of Under Armour and Green Thumb Industries. In October 2022, he announced he would use a blind trust to hold his assets and resign from all board positions if elected governor, and in May 2023, finalized his trust, becoming the first governor to do so since Bob Ehrlich. In May 2025, after conflict of interest concerns arose during Larry Hogan’s 2024 Senate campaign, Moore signed a bill requiring future governors to place their assets in a blind trust or sign a non-participation agreement. He authored several books, including "The Other Wes Moore," published by Spiegel & Grau in April 2010, which explores the lives of two young Baltimore boys with the same name and race but different paths; a film adaptation was announced in 2012 with Oprah Winfrey as executive producer and in 2021 by Unanimous Media, though no film has been produced as of June 2022. In January 2015, he published "The Work," and in November 2016, released "This Way Home," a young adult novel about a high school basketball player who refuses to join a local gang. In March 2020, he co-wrote "Five Days: The Fiery Reckoning of an American City," which examines the 2015 Baltimore protests from the perspectives of eight Baltimoreans. Moore first expressed interest in politics in 1996 and first mentioned running for governor in 2006, later stating in 2020 that the idea became real when he was about to leave Robin Hood. He gave a speech at the 2008 Democratic National Convention supporting Barack Obama and said in 2013 he had no interest in public office, though Attorney General Doug Gansler considered naming him as a running mate in 2014. In April 2015, following the Baltimore protests, he said the demonstrations were "a long time coming" and that Baltimore "must seize this moment to redress systemic problems and grow"; he attended Freddie Gray’s funeral but left early to speak in Boston, later expressing guilt for being absent. On the eighth anniversary of Gray’s death in April 2023, he tweeted that Gray’s death was a turning point for the city. In February 2017, Governor Larry Hogan nominated him to serve on the University System of Maryland Board of Regents; in October 2020, he joined the transition team for Baltimore mayor-elect Brandon Scott; in January 2021, Speaker Adrienne A. Jones consulted with him to develop a "black agenda" to address racial inequalities in housing, health, banking, government, and private corporations. In April 2022, CNN accused him of embellishing his childhood and upbringing; he created a website to rebut the claims. In December 2025, the Washington Free Beacon accused him of exaggerating details in his 2006 White House fellowship application, including claiming to have graduated Oxford a year and a half earlier than he did, not submitting a thesis, working toward a doctorate, and being a "foremost expert" on Islamic extremism with four articles and two books on radical Islam in Latin America. A spokesperson for Moore disputed the claims, stating he submitted his thesis, though his office could not locate the four articles; Julia Paolitto of Oxford clarified that submitting a thesis to the Bodleian Library was not required for the MLitt program but was required for degree conferment, which Moore did not have. When asked about the report, Moore described it as a distraction and declined to release his thesis, saying he would not spend time retrieving a paper from 20 years ago due to a right-wing blog. In February 2021, Moore announced he was considering a run for governor in 2022, launching his campaign on June 7, 2021, with the slogan "leave no one behind" and emphasizing "work, wages, and wealth"; his running mate was Aruna Miller, a former state delegate. He received endorsements from House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer, Angela Alsobrooks, Oprah Winfrey, and former Governor Parris Glendening, as well as the Maryland State Education Association and VoteVets.org. On April 6, 2022, he filed a complaint with the Maryland State Board of Elections against John King Jr.'s campaign, accusing an unidentified party of disseminating false and disparaging information via email and social media, and suggesting King may have been responsible; the King campaign denied it, and in April 2024, King’s campaign was fined $2,000 after prosecutors linked the email to Joseph O'Hearn, his campaign manager. Moore won the Democratic primary on July 19, 2022, defeating Tom Perez and Peter Franchot with 32.4% of the vote. During the general election, he campaigned twice with President Joe Biden and highlighted his military service while criticizing Republican nominee Dan Cox for his role in the January 6 Capitol attack. He defeated Cox and became Maryland’s first Black governor and the first veteran elected to the office since William Donald Schaefer. In December 2022, he was elected finance chair of the Democratic Governors Association. On September 9, 2025, he announced he would run for re-election. He was sworn in on January 18, 2023, taking the oath of office on a Bible owned by Frederick Douglass and his grandfather’s Bible. The day before, he participated in a wreath-laying ceremony at the Kunta Kinte-Alex Haley Memorial to acknowledge his journey to becoming the third elected Black governor in U.S. history. Later that night, he held a celebratory event at the Baltimore Convention Center. As governor, he testified for several of his administration’s bills, making him the first governor to do so since Martin O'Malley. His legislative priorities during his first term included establishing a "service year option" for high school graduates, removing regulations on new housing development, and supporting military families through health care benefits, tax cuts, and employment opportunities. He has sought to reverse or revise decisions by his predecessors, including the cancellation of the Baltimore Red Line, the withholding of state funding for training abortion care providers, and plans to expand portions of the Capital Beltway and Interstate 270 using high-occupancy toll lanes. After the Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse during his tenure, he supported and signed legislation providing financial assistance to workers and businesses affected by the port closure and urged Congress to pass federal legislation to cover the bridge’s rebuilding costs. In December 2024, President Joe Biden signed a continuing resolution that fully funded the bridge replacement. In December 2025, The Baltimore Banner reported that Moore and members of his administration used Google Chat with the "History is Off" function activated, which auto-deletes messages after 24 hours; state law requires state government units to define which records must be saved and which do not. The Moore administration defended the use of self-deleting messages, claiming it was an "approved internal messaging feature" and "complies fully with all Maryland records laws and retention policies."

The Francis Scott Key Bridge collapse occurred during Moore's tenure, after which he supported and signed into law legislation to provide financial assistance to workers and businesses affected by the subsequent closure of the Port of Baltimore. Following the disaster, Moore has urged Congress to pass legislation that would have the federal government cover the costs of rebuilding the bridge. In December 2024, President Joe Biden signed into law a continuing resolution bill that included a provision to fully fund the Francis Scott Key Bridge replacement. In December 2025, The Baltimore Banner reported that Moore and several members of his administration were, at times, communicating using the Google Chat platform with the "History is Off" function activated, which auto-deletes messages after 24 hours. State law requires that every unit of the state government have policies defining which records need to be saved and which don't. In response to the Banner's findings, the Moore administration defended its use of self-deleting messages, saying that it was an "approved internal messaging feature" and "complies fully with all Maryland records laws and retention policies," but later said that the governor's office would work with the attorney general of Maryland to create a "uniform retention policy" across the executive branch. Moore met Dawn Flythe in Washington, D.C. in 2002. They moved to the Riverside community in Baltimore in 2006. The couple eloped in Las Vegas while he was on a brief leave from Afghanistan and were married by an Elvis impersonator. Their official wedding ceremony was held on July 6, 2007. They have two children, born in 2011 and 2013. In late 2008, the Moores moved from Riverside to Guilford, where they lived until Moore's election as governor in 2022. From 2015 to 2023, he attended services at the Southern Baptist Church in east Baltimore. They reside in Government House, the official residence of the Maryland governor and First Family in Annapolis, Maryland. Moore holds honorary degrees from Lafayette College, Skidmore College, Lincoln University, and the University of the Commonwealth Caribbean. He is a member of the Sons of the American Revolution; his ancestor Prince Ames served in the Massachusetts Militia in the Revolutionary War. Moore is a fan of the Baltimore Ravens, Baltimore Orioles, and New York Knicks. In June 2013, a Baltimore Sun investigation alleged that Moore was improperly receiving homestead property tax credits and owed back taxes to the city of Baltimore. Moore told The Sun that he was unaware of any issues with the home's taxes and wanted to pay what he owed immediately. In October 2022, Baltimore Brew reported that Moore had not paid any water and sewage charges since March 2021, owing $21,200 to the city of Baltimore.
